claim: Mice carrying a homozygous double deletion of Firre and Dxz4 are viable and fertile.
source: We found that homozygous mice of all three strains are viable and fertile, and by crossing males and females carrying a homozygous double deletion we observed the expected litter sizes and sex ratios (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed litter sizes and sex ratios from breeding experiments with homozygous double deletion mice.

claim: Deletion of Firre and Dxz4 loci does not affect random X chromosome inactivation in vivo.
source: In agreement with previous in vitro studies, we find that the loss of these loci in vivo does not affect random XCI.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq and allele-specific analysis data from F1 crosses showing no impact on XCI.

claim: Deletion of Firre and Dxz4 loci does not affect imprinted X chromosome inactivation.
source: Moreover, by studying the placenta and the visceral yolk sac we were able to show for the first time that loss of these loci also does not affect imprinted XCI.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data from placenta and visceral yolk sac showing no dysregulated X-linked genes except Firre itself.

claim: Firre is exclusively expressed from the active X chromosome in imprinted XCI.
source: We did not detect Firre expression if the deletion was inherited maternally, while we detected Firre wildtype expression levels in the paternal deletion, demonstrating that Firre is exclusively expressed from the Xa (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing Firre expression patterns in placenta and visceral yolk sac from reciprocal crosses.

claim: Firre does not escape imprinted X chromosome inactivation.
source: Thus, in contrast to previous reports that identified Firre as a gene that escapes XCI in cell lines that model random XCI (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Andergassen et al., 2017; Berletch et al., 2015), we found that Firre does not escape imprinted XCI.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing Firre is only expressed from the active X in imprinted XCI, and cites previous studies showing escape in random XCI.

claim: Firre was previously identified as a gene that escapes XCI in cell lines modeling random XCI.
source: Thus, in contrast to previous reports that identified Firre as a gene that escapes XCI in cell lines that model random XCI (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Andergassen et al., 2017; Berletch et al., 2015), we found that Firre does not escape imprinted XCI.
evidence: The manuscript cites three previous studies that reported Firre escape from XCI.

claim: Deletion of Dxz4 does not impact Firre gene expression in random or imprinted X inactivation.
source: Remarkably, in the Dxz4 SKO we detected a Firre wildtype pattern, suggesting that disruption of the superloop between the two loci or the absence of megadomains has no impact on Firre gene expression in either random or imprinted X inactivation (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing normal Firre expression in Dxz4 single knockout mice.

claim: Xist expression levels are not changed in the absence of Firre and Dxz4 loci.
source: We did not observe changes in Xist expression levels in the absence of these loci (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing Xist expression levels in knockout strains.

claim: Firre is the only differentially expressed gene on the X chromosome in the placenta when Firre and Dxz4 are deleted.
source: To identify dysregulated X-linked genes for each possible combination of the deletion, we performed differential expression analysis and found that the only dysregulated gene on the X chromosome was the lncRNA Firre (FDR ≤ 0.1 and |log2FC| ≥ 1), suggesting that the mega-structures and the Firre lncRNA have no impact on imprinted XCI (Figure 3A right panel, Supplementary file 1 sheet A-B).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis results from placenta RNA-seq data.

claim: The mega-structures and Firre lncRNA have no impact on imprinted XCI.
source: To identify dysregulated X-linked genes for each possible combination of the deletion, we performed differential expression analysis and found that the only dysregulated gene on the X chromosome was the lncRNA Firre (FDR ≤ 0.1 and |log2FC| ≥ 1), suggesting that the mega-structures and the Firre lncRNA have no impact on imprinted XCI (Figure 3A right panel, Supplementary file 1 sheet A-B).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the lack of dysregulated X-linked genes (except Firre itself) in differential expression analysis.

claim: Few autosomal genes are dysregulated in the DKO that were not changed in the SKO in the placenta.
source: Notably, by using the same criteria we detected only a few autosomal genes dysregulated in the DKO that were not changed in the SKO, suggesting that the mega-structures and the lncRNA Firre have no impact on autosomal gene regulation in the placenta (Supplementary file 1 sheet A-B).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis comparing DKO and SKO strains in placenta.

claim: DNA methylation levels on CpG islands are not affected in the absence of mega-structures or Firre lncRNA.
source: DNA methylation levels on CpG islands were also not affected in the absence of the mega-structures or the lncRNA Firre, suggesting that the epigenetic processes involved in establishing the inactive X proceed normally without either (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1 sheet C).
evidence: The manuscript presents RRBS data showing CpG island methylation levels in wildtype and knockout placentas.

claim: The epigenetic processes involved in establishing the inactive X proceed normally without Firre and Dxz4.
source: DNA methylation levels on CpG islands were also not affected in the absence of the mega-structures or the lncRNA Firre, suggesting that the epigenetic processes involved in establishing the inactive X proceed normally without either (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1 sheet C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that DNA methylation levels are unchanged in knockout mice.

claim: The median allelic ratio of all X-linked genes is unchanged regardless of whether deletions are on Xa or Xi.
source: We found that the median allelic ratio of all the X-linked genes was unchanged regardless if the deletions were on Xa or Xi (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific expression analysis from RNA-seq data.

claim: Deletion of Firre and Dxz4 loci on Xa or Xi does not result in increased escape in the placenta or visceral yolk sac.
source: Moreover, deletion of these loci on the Xa or Xi did not result in increased escape in the placenta or visceral yolk sac (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1 sheet D-E).
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific expression analysis showing no change in escape patterns.

claim: Allele-specific analysis revealed strain-specific escaping with a greater number of genes escaping from CAST Xi compared to Bl6 Xi.
source: Of note, allele-specific analysis revealed strain-specific escaping with a greater number of gene escape from CAST Xi compared to Bl6 Xi (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1 sheet D-E).
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific expression analysis comparing escape patterns between strains.

claim: Random XCI in the brain shows expected XCI skewing ratios in the presence of Firre and Dxz4 deletions.
source: Random XCI in the brain also did not appear to be affected, since we detect the expected XCI skewing ratios in the presence of the deletions, a well-documented effect in female cells from crosses between Bl6 and CAST that results in the predominant inactivation of the Bl6 X chromosome (Calaway et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B left panel).
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific expression analysis from brain RNA-seq data and cites a previous study documenting XCI skewing.

claim: Female cells from crosses between Bl6 and CAST show predominant inactivation of the Bl6 X chromosome.
source: Random XCI in the brain also did not appear to be affected, since we detect the expected XCI skewing ratios in the presence of the deletions, a well-documented effect in female cells from crosses between Bl6 and CAST that results in the predominant inactivation of the Bl6 X chromosome (Calaway et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B left panel).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and presents data consistent with this effect.

claim: DKO animals show significant skewing of Xist allelic ratios.
source: However, our DKO animals show significant skewing of the Xist allelic ratios (t-test, FDR-adjusted p-value=0.0108) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B right panel), suggesting that the Bl6 chromosome is further biased toward silencing in mice lacking both Firre and Dxz4.
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis of Xist allelic ratios from RNA-seq data.

claim: The Bl6 chromosome is further biased toward silencing in mice lacking both Firre and Dxz4.
source: However, our DKO animals show significant skewing of the Xist allelic ratios (t-test, FDR-adjusted p-value=0.0108) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B right panel), suggesting that the Bl6 chromosome is further biased toward silencing in mice lacking both Firre and Dxz4.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observed significant skewing of Xist allelic ratios.

claim: Autosomal genes show expected biallelic ratios across all samples.
source: In contrast, for autosomal genes we detect the expected biallelic ratios across all samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific expression analysis for autosomal genes.

claim: Most dysregulated genes in adult organs show organ-specific expression changes, primarily on autosomes.
source: We then performed differential expression analysis of spleen, brain, kidney, heart, lung and liver and found that most of the dysregulated genes show organ-specific expression changes, primarily on autosomes (autosomes: 98.15% n = 372 chrX: 1.85% n = 7), with only a few overlapping genes across organs (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1 sheet F).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis from RNA-seq data of six adult organs.

claim: 98.15% of dysregulated genes in adult organs are on autosomes and 1.85% are on the X chromosome.
source: We then performed differential expression analysis of spleen, brain, kidney, heart, lung and liver and found that most of the dysregulated genes show organ-specific expression changes, primarily on autosomes (autosomes: 98.15% n = 372 chrX: 1.85% n = 7), with only a few overlapping genes across organs (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1 sheet F).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of differentially expressed genes by chromosome.

claim: The highest number of differentially expressed genes was detected in the spleen (n = 239).
source: The highest number of differentially expressed genes was detected in the spleen (n = 239, compared to the rest of the organs that on average had 30 dysregulated genes).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis results across multiple organs.

claim: The rest of the organs had on average 30 dysregulated genes.
source: The highest number of differentially expressed genes was detected in the spleen (n = 239, compared to the rest of the organs that on average had 30 dysregulated genes).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis results across multiple organs.

claim: In the liver, 15 megadomain-dependent, 4 superloop-dependent, and 4 Firre locus-dependent genes were identified.
source: We first used this approach for the liver, an organ with a low number of differentially expressed genes in the DKO, and identified 15 megadomain, four superloop, and 4 Firre locus dependent genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1 sheet G).
evidence: The manuscript presents categorization of dysregulated genes based on comparison across knockout strains.

claim: Xist shows megadomain dependence and is significantly upregulated in the DKO brain and kidney, as well as in the Dxz4 SKO spleen.
source: Notably, without applying the fold change cutoff, we observe megadomain dependence of Xist, which is significantly upregulated in the DKO brain and kidney, as well as in the Dxz4 SKO spleen (mean upregulation 30%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis showing Xist upregulation in specific organs and strains.

claim: Xist shows a mean upregulation of 30% in megadomain-dependent contexts.
source: Notably, without applying the fold change cutoff, we observe megadomain dependence of Xist, which is significantly upregulated in the DKO brain and kidney, as well as in the Dxz4 SKO spleen (mean upregulation 30%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of Xist expression changes.

claim: In the spleen, 7 megadomain-dependent (4%), 26 superloop-dependent (14.8%), and 142 Firre locus-dependent (81.1%) genes were identified.
source: We next applied the same approach to the spleen, the organ with the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the DKO, and identified seven megadomain (4%), 26 superloop (14.8%) and 142 Firre locus (81.1%) dependent genes (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1 sheet H).
evidence: The manuscript presents categorization of dysregulated genes in the spleen based on comparison across knockout strains.

claim: The Firre locus-dependent gene set contains only downregulated genes.
source: The Firre locus dependent gene set—the largest group—contains only downregulated genes, including the gene Ypel4 that was previously described to form interchromosomal interactions with the Firre locus (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Maass et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis showing directionality of gene expression changes.

claim: Ypel4 was previously described to form interchromosomal interactions with the Firre locus.
source: The Firre locus dependent gene set—the largest group—contains only downregulated genes, including the gene Ypel4 that was previously described to form interchromosomal interactions with the Firre locus (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Maass et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites two previous studies that reported this interaction.

claim: The top Firre SKO and DKO enriched gene sets are almost identical, sharing downregulated gene sets involved in chromosome structure and segregation.
source: By gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), we find that the top Firre SKO and DKO enriched gene sets are almost identical, sharing downregulated gene sets involved in chromosome structure and segregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1 sheet I).
evidence: The manuscript presents GSEA analysis results comparing Firre SKO and DKO.

claim: Genes extracted from enriched gene sets identified in Firre SKO and DKO share a similar pattern of downregulation, which was not observed in the Dxz4 SKO.
source: Genes extracted from the enriched gene sets identified in the Firre SKO and DKO share a similar pattern of downregulation, which was not observed in the Dxz4 SKO (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparison of gene expression patterns across knockout strains.

claim: Fold changes in Firre SKO and DKO are strongly correlated (spearman rho = 0.87, p-value<2.2*10−16).
source: In addition, fold changes in Firre SKO and DKO are strongly correlated (spearman rho = 0.87, p-value<2.2*10−16), indicating that the Firre locus is the main driver for downregulation of these gene sets (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical correlation analysis of fold changes between strains.

claim: The Firre locus is the main driver for downregulation of chromosome structure and segregation gene sets.
source: In addition, fold changes in Firre SKO and DKO are strongly correlated (spearman rho = 0.87, p-value<2.2*10−16), indicating that the Firre locus is the main driver for downregulation of these gene sets (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the strong correlation of fold changes between Firre SKO and DKO.

claim: A similar pattern of downregulation is observed in DKO male spleens as in females.
source: To test whether this molecular phenotype can be uncoupled form X inactivation, we performed the same analysis in DKO male spleens. We found a similar pattern of downregulation as observed in females (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis from male DKO spleens.

claim: The Firre locus acts independently of X inactivation as the main driver of autosomal expression signatures.
source: Taken together these findings point to the Firre locus, independently of X inactivation, as the main driver of these autosomal expression signatures.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that similar expression patterns occur in males (which do not undergo XCI) and females.

claim: The loss of Firre and Dxz4 loci does not affect long-term maintenance of the Xi chromosome.
source: The lack of dysregulated X-linked genes in adult organs suggests that these mega-structures may also not be important for long-term maintenance of the Xi chromosome.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that X-linked genes are not dysregulated in adult organs.

claim: Deletion of Firre and Dxz4 loci results in reproducible organ-specific expression changes on autosomes.
source: Remarkably, deletion of these loci results in reproducible organ-specific expression changes on autosomes suggesting that structural changes of the Barr body may lead to autosomal gene dysregulation.
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis showing organ-specific autosomal gene dysregulation.

claim: Structural changes of the Barr body may lead to autosomal gene dysregulation.
source: Remarkably, deletion of these loci results in reproducible organ-specific expression changes on autosomes suggesting that structural changes of the Barr body may lead to autosomal gene dysregulation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on a possible mechanism based on observed gene dysregulation patterns.

claim: Crosstalk between autosomes and the X chromosome has been proposed as a mechanism for X inactivation counting.
source: Indeed, crosstalk between autosomes and the X chromosome has been proposed as a mechanism for X inactivation counting (Rastan, 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study proposing this mechanism.

claim: The largest transcriptional effect on autosomes is Firre locus-dependent and X inactivation-independent.
source: The largest transcriptional effect on autosomes is Firre locus-dependent and X inactivation-independent, suggesting a role for the Firre RNA or DNA locus in autosomal gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis showing Firre locus-dependent effects in both males and females.

claim: The Firre RNA or DNA locus has a role in autosomal gene regulation.
source: The largest transcriptional effect on autosomes is Firre locus-dependent and X inactivation-independent, suggesting a role for the Firre RNA or DNA locus in autosomal gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation of Firre locus-dependent autosomal gene dysregulation.

claim: The major function of dysregulated genes appears to be in ontologies associated with chromosome structure and segregation.
source: The major function of these dysregulated genes appears to be in ontologies associated with chromosome structure and segregation, which is in line with the known role for Firre lncRNA in nuclear organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript presents GSEA analysis results and cites a previous study on Firre's role in nuclear organization.

claim: Firre lncRNA has a known role in nuclear organization.
source: The major function of these dysregulated genes appears to be in ontologies associated with chromosome structure and segregation, which is in line with the known role for Firre lncRNA in nuclear organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that established this role.

claim: The X-linked loci Firre and Dxz4 are involved in autosomal gene regulation rather than XCI biology in vivo.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that the X-linked loci Firre and Dxz4, are involved in autosomal gene regulation rather than XCI biology in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the pattern of autosomal dysregulation without X-linked gene dysregulation.

claim: In female mammals, one of the two X chromosomes is inactivated to compensate for gene dosage between males and females.
source: In female mammals, one of the two X chromosomes is inactivated to compensate for gene dosage between males and females (Lyon, 1961), a process termed X-chromosome inactivation (XCI).
evidence: The manuscript cites a foundational study on X chromosome inactivation.

claim: In mice, there are two successive waves of XCI: imprinted and random.
source: In mice, there are two successive waves of XCI: imprinted and random.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mouse XCI.

claim: Imprinted XCI starts early in development by specifically inactivating the paternal X chromosome.
source: Imprinted XCI starts early in development by specifically inactivating the paternal X chromosome (Xp) (Kay et al., 1994; Okamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites two previous studies that established this mechanism.

claim: The paternal X chromosome remains silenced in extra-embryonic lineages.
source: While the Xp remains silenced in extra-embryonic lineages (Takagi and Sasaki, 1975), it is reactivated in the embryo during implantation, followed by random XCI (Mak et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that established this pattern.

claim: The paternal X chromosome is reactivated in the embryo during implantation, followed by random XCI.
source: While the Xp remains silenced in extra-embryonic lineages (Takagi and Sasaki, 1975), it is reactivated in the embryo during implantation, followed by random XCI (Mak et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that established this developmental pattern.

claim: The inactive X chromosome is epigenetically maintained throughout cell division as a compact chromatin structure known as the 'Barr body'.
source: After this decision has been made, the inactive X (Xi) chromosome is epigenetically maintained throughout cell division as a compact chromatin structure known as the 'Barr body' (Barr and Bertram, 1949).
evidence: The manuscript cites the foundational study that identified the Barr body.

claim: The Xi folds into two megadomains and forms a network of long-range interactions termed superloops that are directed by the non-coding loci Firre and Dxz4.
source: Recent studies using chromosome conformation capture (3C) based methods have identified that the Xi folds into two megadomains and forms a network of long-range interactions termed superloops that are directed by the non-coding loci Firre and Dxz4 (Rao et al., 2014; Horakova et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites three previous studies that identified these structures.

claim: Deletion of Dxz4 in cell lines leads to the loss of both megadomain and superloop.
source: Deletion of Dxz4 in cell lines leads to the loss of both megadomain and superloop (Giorgetti et al., 2016; Bonora et al., 2018; Froberg et al., 2018; Darrow et al., 2016), while deletion of Firre alone disrupts the superloop but has no impact on megadomain formation (Froberg et al., 2018; Barutcu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites four previous studies that demonstrated this effect.

claim: Deletion of Firre alone disrupts the superloop but has no impact on megadomain formation.
source: Deletion of Dxz4 in cell lines leads to the loss of both megadomain and superloop (Giorgetti et al., 2016; Bonora et al., 2018; Froberg et al., 2018; Darrow et al., 2016), while deletion of Firre alone disrupts the superloop but has no impact on megadomain formation (Froberg et al., 2018; Barutcu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites two previous studies that demonstrated this effect.

claim: The Firre locus is transcribed into the long non-coding RNA Firre that escapes XCI and plays a role in nuclear organization.
source: Moreover, the Firre locus is transcribed into the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Firre that escapes XCI and plays a role in nuclear organization (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014; Andergassen et al., 2017; Berletch et al., 2015; Bergmann et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites five previous studies that established these properties of Firre.

claim: Recent studies in human and mouse cell line models found that deletion of Firre and Dxz4 have minimal impact on X chromosome biology beyond the loss of mega-structures.
source: Recent studies in human and mouse cell line models of random XCI, found that deletion of these elements have minimal impact on X chromosome biology beyond the loss of these structures, though the phenotypic consequences of their deletion throughout mammalian development have not been addressed (Giorgetti et al., 2016; Bonora et al., 2018; Froberg et al., 2018; Darrow et al., 2016; Barutcu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites five previous cell line studies that demonstrated this finding.

claim: The phenotypic consequences of Firre and Dxz4 deletion throughout mammalian development have not been previously addressed.
source: Recent studies in human and mouse cell line models of random XCI, found that deletion of these elements have minimal impact on X chromosome biology beyond the loss of these structures, though the phenotypic consequences of their deletion throughout mammalian development have not been addressed (Giorgetti et al., 2016; Bonora et al., 2018; Froberg et al., 2018; Darrow et al., 2016; Barutcu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in previous research based on cited studies.

claim: Three knockout mouse strains were generated: Firre SKO, Dxz4 SKO, and Firre-Dxz4 DKO.
source: In order to test the in vivo role of Firre and Dxz4 loci both individually and in combination, we generated three knockout (KO) mouse strains: two carrying a single locus deletion (SKO) of either Firre (Lewandowski et al., 2019) or Dxz4 and one carrying a double locus deletion (DKO) of Firre in conjunction with Dxz4 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of these mouse strains.

claim: The targeted regions were previously reported to disrupt the superloop and megadomain structures.
source: Notably, we targeted the regions that have been previously reported to disrupt the superloop (Barutcu et al., 2018) and megadomain structures (Bonora et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites two previous studies that identified these regions.

claim: All founder mice were screened by PCR and identified mutants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
source: All founder mice were screened by PCR using primers that span the deleted region and identified mutants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C, Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methods used to identify and confirm mutations.

claim: Homozygous mice of all three strains are viable and fertile.
source: We found that homozygous mice of all three strains are viable and fertile, and by crossing males and females carrying a homozygous double deletion we observed the expected litter sizes and sex ratios (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports breeding outcomes from the knockout strains.

claim: Crossing homozygous DKO males and females resulted in expected litter sizes and sex ratios.
source: We found that homozygous mice of all three strains are viable and fertile, and by crossing males and females carrying a homozygous double deletion we observed the expected litter sizes and sex ratios (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents breeding data showing normal litter sizes and sex ratios.

claim: Firre expression is approximately half of wildtype levels in Firre SKO and DKO female brains.
source: We then investigated the Firre expression level in Firre SKO and DKO female brains, and detected approximately half of the wildtype levels as expected for random XCI (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing Firre expression levels in knockout brains.

claim: Approximately half of wildtype Firre expression levels is expected for random XCI.
source: We then investigated the Firre expression level in Firre SKO and DKO female brains, and detected approximately half of the wildtype levels as expected for random XCI (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript implies this expectation based on the logic that one X chromosome is inactivated in random XCI.

claim: Firre is approximately 4 times higher expressed from the Bl6 allele compared to the CAST allele.
source: Notably, Firre is approximately 4 times higher expressed from the Bl6 allele compared to the CAST allele, as observed by comparing the expression levels between the forward cross (Xa Bl6) and reverse cross (Xa CAST) in the placenta and visceral yolk sac.
evidence: The manuscript presents this observation from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The major urinary protein gene cluster shows high interindividual expression variation.
source: The major urinary protein gene cluster, which was previously found to show high interindividual expression variation (Thoß et al., 2015) shows megadomain-dependent upregulation (right).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and presents data showing this pattern.

claim: The major urinary protein gene cluster shows megadomain-dependent upregulation.
source: The major urinary protein gene cluster, which was previously found to show high interindividual expression variation (Thoß et al., 2015) shows megadomain-dependent upregulation (right).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis showing this pattern in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Across all strains carrying the Firre locus deletion, the enriched gene sets share the majority of genes with the greatest degree of dysregulation.
source: Across all strains carrying the Firre locus deletion, the enriched gene sets share the majority of genes with the greatest degree of dysregulation (Supplementary file 1 sheet I).
evidence: The manuscript presents GSEA analysis results comparing strains with Firre deletion.

claim: The relationship between dysregulated genes and chromosome structure/segregation ontologies points to an RNA dependent role on autosomal gene regulation.
source: This relationship points to an RNA dependent role, which may be either direct or indirect, on autosomal gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the mechanism based on the observed gene ontology enrichment.

claim: The RNA dependent role on autosomal gene regulation may be either direct or indirect.
source: This relationship points to an RNA dependent role, which may be either direct or indirect, on autosomal gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: The Firre deletion mouse has a deletion at mm10: chrX:50,555,286–50,637,116.
source: The Firre deletion mouse (deletion mm10: chrX:50,555,286–50,637,116) was generated by inserting LoxP sites flanking the Firre gene body into JM8A ESCs (Bl6 background) (Hacisuleyman et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript provides the genomic coordinates of the deletion.

claim: The Dxz4 single deletion strain has a deletion at chrX:75,721,164–75,764,733 mm10.
source: The Dxz4 single deletion strain (chrX:75,721,164–75,764,733 mm10) was generated by co-injecting Cas9 mRNA (200 ng/µl) together with two guide RNA's that span the Dxz4 locus (50 ng/µl each) into pronuclear stage 3 (PN3) zygotes isolated after mating super ovulated B6D2F1 female mice (Jackson labs) with Bl6 males as previously described (Wang et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript provides the genomic coordinates and generation method for the Dxz4 deletion.

claim: The Firre-Dxz4 double deletion strain has a Dxz4 deletion at chrX:75,720,836–75,764,839.
source: The Firre-Dxz4 double deletion strain (Dxz4 deletion chrX:75,720,836–75,764,839, Firre deletion same as for Firre SKO), was generated by piezo-assisted Intracytoplasmic sperm injection of Firre SKO sperm into B6D2F1 oocytes (protocol described in Yoshida and Perry, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript provides the genomic coordinates for the Dxz4 deletion in the DKO strain.

claim: Founder mice of the Dxz4 SKO and DKO strains were backcrossed at least two times with C57BL/6J to remove strain background or CRISPR-Cas9 off-target effects.
source: Founder mice of the Dxz4 SKO and DKO strains were backcrossed at least two times with C57BL/6J to remove strain background or CRISPR-Cas9 off-target effects.
evidence: The manuscript describes the breeding strategy to control for confounding factors.

claim: All wildtype control mice were obtained from backcrossing of founder mice with C57BL/6J to match the KO strain background.
source: In order to control for strain background, all wildtype control mice were obtained from backcrossing of founder mice with C57BL/6J to match the KO strain background.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design to control for genetic background.

claim: The same organs were collected from males to test the role of Firre and Dxz4 on the X chromosome outside of XCI biology.
source: We collected the same organs from males to test the role of these loci on the X chromosome outside of XCI biology.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design to separate XCI-dependent from XCI-independent effects.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of sequenced samples confirmed the identity of the tissues.
source: Unsupervised clustering of the sequenced samples confirmed the identity of the tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents clustering analysis as a quality control measure.

claim: A transcriptomic bodymap was generated from adult females carrying a homozygous double Firre-Dxz4 deletion.
source: To address whether the absence of both the mega-structures and Firre RNA has an impact on gene expression in an organ-specific manner, we generated a transcriptomic bodymap from adult females carrying a homozygous double Firre-Dxz4 deletion (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of a multi-organ transcriptomic dataset.

claim: Differential expression analysis was performed on spleen, brain, kidney, heart, lung and liver.
source: We then performed differential expression analysis of spleen, brain, kidney, heart, lung and liver and found that most of the dysregulated genes show organ-specific expression changes, primarily on autosomes (autosomes: 98.15% n = 372 chrX: 1.85% n = 7), with only a few overlapping genes across organs (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1 sheet F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical approach for the bodymap data.

claim: Spleen and liver were sequenced from independently generated Firre and Dxz4 SKO animals to validate and categorize dysregulated genes.
source: To validate and categorize the dysregulated genes identified in the DKO into superloop, megadomain, and Firre locus-dependent gene sets, we sequenced the spleen and the liver from independently generated Firre and Dxz4 SKO animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design for validation studies.

claim: Dysregulated gene sets shared across all three strains are superloop specific.
source: We hypothesized that dysregulated gene sets that are: (1) shared across the three strains are superloop specific (2) shared between Dxz4 SKO and DKO are megadomain-dependent and (3) shared between Firre SKO and the DKO are Firre locus specific.
evidence: The manuscript describes the logical framework for categorizing dysregulated genes.

claim: Dysregulated gene sets shared between Dxz4 SKO and DKO are megadomain-dependent.
source: We hypothesized that dysregulated gene sets that are: (1) shared across the three strains are superloop specific (2) shared between Dxz4 SKO and DKO are megadomain-dependent and (3) shared between Firre SKO and the DKO are Firre locus specific.
evidence: The manuscript describes the logical framework for categorizing dysregulated genes.

claim: Dysregulated gene sets shared between Firre SKO and DKO are Firre locus specific.
source: We hypothesized that dysregulated gene sets that are: (1) shared across the three strains are superloop specific (2) shared between Dxz4 SKO and DKO are megadomain-dependent and (3) shared between Firre SKO and the DKO are Firre locus specific.
evidence: The manuscript describes the logical framework for categorizing dysregulated genes.

claim: Genes dysregulated in at least one of the three KO strains where the direction of expression change in either single KO agrees with the DKO were selected for categorization.
source: To identify gene sets for these categories, we selected the genes dysregulated in at least one of the three KO strains where the direction of the expression change in either one of the single KO agrees with that of the DKO (|log2FC| ≥ 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the criteria for gene selection in the categorization analysis.

claim: GSEA analysis was performed on DEseq2 test statistics with all GO gene sets.
source: The GSEA analysis was performed on DEseq2 test statistics with all GO gene sets (c5.all.v6.2.symbols) available from MSigDB (Subramanian et al., 2005) after mapping genes to gene sets by gene symbols.
evidence: The manuscript describes the GSEA methodology and cites the gene set database.

claim: A gene set was called significant in GSEA if the FDR-adjusted p-value is less than or equal to 0.1.
source: A gene set was called significant if the FDR-adjusted p-value (Benjamini and Hochberg method) is less than or equal to 0.1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical threshold for significance in GSEA.

claim: Genes were called differentially expressed if their FDR-adjusted p-values were smaller or equal than 0.1.
source: Genes were called significant if their FDR-adjusted p-values were smaller or equal than 0.1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical threshold for differential expression.

claim: The Allelome.PRO uses characterized single-nucleotide polymorphisms to assign sequencing reads to the corresponding strain in F1 crosses.
source: Allelome.PRO uses the information of characterized single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to assign sequencing reads to the corresponding strain in F1 crosses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the principle of the Allelome.PRO pipeline.

claim: 15,438,314 high confidence SNPs between CAST/EiJ and C57BL6NJ were used for allele-specific analysis.
source: Although we backcrossed all the founder mice to Bl6, to exclude potential strain background confounding effects, we performed the allele-specific analysis using only CAST/Bl6 SNPs where the Bl6 allele was shared between DBA, BALB/C and 129 (Final SNP number: 15,438,314 SNPs).
evidence: The manuscript describes the SNP filtering strategy for allele-specific analysis.

claim: For Allelome.PRO analysis, only SNPs covered by at least two reads were included.
source: For the Allelome.PRO analysis we only included SNPs that are covered by at least two reads by setting the 'minread' parameter to 2.
evidence: The manuscript describes the quality control parameters for allele-specific analysis.

claim: Sequence data and alignments have been submitted to the Gene Expression Omnibus database under accession code GSE127554.
source: Sequence data and alignments have been submitted to the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accession code GSE127554.
evidence: The manuscript provides the data repository accession code.
